Swallow ER capsules whole; with or without food

summary: Diltiazem is a non-dihydropyridine (benzothiazepine) calcium channel blocker that inhibits calcium-ion influx into cardiac and vascular smooth muscle during membrane depolarization. Oral extended-release capsules are indicated for hypertension and for chronic stable angina and angina due to coronary artery spasm; it lowers blood pressure by relaxing vascular smooth muscle and reduces angina by lowering myocardial oxygen demand and dilating coronary arteries. Diltiazem also slows sinoatrial and atrioventricular conduction, which underlies its intravenous use for rate control in atrial fibrillation/flutter and for terminating PSVT. It is both a substrate and inhibitor of CYP3A4, giving it many drug interactions. Contraindications include sick sinus syndrome or high-degree AV block without a pacemaker, systolic BP <90 mm Hg, and acute MI with pulmonary congestion.
indications: Hypertension (oral extended-release; alone or with other antihypertensives)
Management of chronic stable angina (oral extended-release)
Angina due to coronary artery spasm / Prinzmetal's angina (oral extended-release)

Intravenous: temporary control of rapid ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter (not in patients whose AF/flutter is associated with an accessory bypass tract such as WPW or short PR syndrome)
Intravenous: rapid conversion of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT), including AV nodal reentrant and accessory-pathway reciprocating tachycardias, to sinus rhythm

dosage.d: Start 180-240 mg once daily; usual range 240-360 mg once daily; some patients respond to up to 480 mg/day
dosage.t: Maximum antihypertensive effect usually seen by 14 days; schedule adjustments accordingly
dosage.n: Some patients respond to lower starting doses; ER capsules give once-daily dosing

dosage.c: Chronic stable angina / coronary artery spasm (oral extended-release)
dosage.d: Start 120 or 180 mg once daily; may increase up to 480 mg once daily
dosage.t: Titrate over a 7- to 14-day period when necessary
dosage.n: Sublingual nitroglycerin may be used for acute attacks; safely combined with short- and long-acting nitrates

dosage.c: Switching to extended-release from other diltiazem formulations
dosage.d: Use the nearest equivalent total daily dose; some patients need higher doses
dosage.t: Subsequent up- or down-titration as needed; monitor closely
dosage.n: Limited experience above 360 mg; doses up to 540 mg studied in trials

dosage.c: Atrial fibrillation/flutter rate control or PSVT conversion (IV bolus)
dosage.d: Initial 0.25 mg/kg actual body weight over 2 minutes (~20 mg for the average patient); if response inadequate, a second dose of 0.35 mg/kg over 2 minutes (~25 mg average) after 15 minutes; subsequent boluses individualized
dosage.t: Response usually within 3 minutes; maximal heart rate reduction in 2-7 minutes; effect lasts 1-3 hours
dosage.n: Dose low-body-weight patients on a mg/kg basis; some respond to an initial 0.15 mg/kg (shorter duration, limited experience). Do NOT use in AF/flutter with an accessory bypass tract (WPW or short PR syndrome). Use IV diltiazem injection, not the oral ER capsule

dosage.c: Atrial fibrillation/flutter rate control - continued (IV infusion)
dosage.d: After the bolus, begin at 10 mg/hour (some patients maintain response at 5 mg/hour); may increase in 5 mg/hour increments up to 15 mg/hour as needed
dosage.t: May be maintained for up to 24 hours
dosage.n: Infusion duration beyond 24 hours and rates above 15 mg/hour are not recommended (not studied); requires continuous ECG and frequent BP monitoring. Use IV diltiazem injection, not the oral ER capsule

admin: Swallow extended-release capsules whole; may be taken with or without food
Use slow titration when combined with other agents affecting cardiac contractility or conduction (beta-blockers, digitalis)
Sublingual nitroglycerin may be taken as needed for acute anginal attacks during therapy
Adjust dose of diltiazem or concomitant antihypertensives when adding one to the other (additive BP effect)
moa: Diltiazem is a calcium-ion cellular influx inhibitor (slow-channel blocker) that inhibits the influx of calcium ions into cardiac and vascular smooth muscle during membrane depolarization. In hypertension it acts primarily by relaxing vascular smooth muscle, decreasing peripheral vascular resistance. In angina it increases exercise tolerance by reducing myocardial oxygen demand (via lower heart rate and systemic BP at submaximal and maximal workloads) and is a potent dilator of epicardial and subendocardial coronary arteries, inhibiting spontaneous and ergonovine-induced coronary spasm. It decreases sinoatrial and atrioventricular conduction, prolonging AH conduction time and AV node refractory periods, which provides rate control in atrial fibrillation/flutter and terminates PSVT. No reflex tachycardia accompanies its chronic antihypertensive effect.

absolute: Sick sinus syndrome except with a functioning ventricular pacemaker
Second- or third-degree AV block except with a functioning ventricular pacemaker
Acute myocardial infarction with pulmonary congestion documented by x-ray on admission
Intravenous use: atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter associated with an accessory bypass tract (e.g., WPW or short PR syndrome)
relative: Preexisting impairment of left ventricular function / congestive heart failure (worsening reported)
Concomitant beta-blockers, especially with LV dysfunction or conduction abnormalities
Concomitant CYP3A4 substrates, inhibitors, or inducers (significant PK interactions)
monitor: Heart rate and ECG (AV block, bradycardia) especially with beta-blockers or digitalis
Hepatic function (transaminases, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin), particularly first 1-8 weeks

preg: There are no well-controlled studies in pregnant women; use diltiazem only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. In mice, rats, and rabbits, doses 5 to 10 times the human therapeutic dose (mg/kg basis) caused embryo and fetal lethality and, in some studies, skeletal abnormalities; perinatal/postnatal studies showed an increased incidence of stillbirths at doses 20 times the human dose or greater.
lact: Diltiazem is excreted in human milk, and one report suggests milk concentrations may approximate serum levels. If use of diltiazem is deemed essential, institute an alternative method of infant feeding.
renal: Diltiazem is extensively metabolized by the liver and excreted by the kidneys and in bile; monitor renal function at regular intervals. No specific renal dose reduction is given in the label, but patients on CYP3A4-substrate drugs, especially with renal and/or hepatic impairment, may need dose adjustment when diltiazem is started or stopped. Diltiazem does not appear to be removed by peritoneal or hemodialysis.
hepatic: Diltiazem is extensively metabolized by the liver (CYP3A4); monitor hepatic function at regular intervals. Mild, often transient transaminase elevations occur and may resolve despite continued therapy; rare significant elevations of alkaline phosphatase, LDH, SGOT, SGPT and other findings consistent with acute hepatic injury occur early (1-8 weeks) and are reversible on discontinuation. High doses produced reversible hepatic damage in animal studies. Use caution in hepatic impairment and adjust for affected CYP3A4 substrates.

major: Beta-blockers (additive AV conduction effects; propranolol bioavailability increased ~50% - adjust dose; caution with LV dysfunction)
Digitalis/digoxin (additive AV conduction slowing; digoxin levels increased ~20% - monitor levels)
Ivabradine (increased exposure; exacerbates bradycardia and conduction disturbances - avoid)
CYP3A4-metabolized statins (increased AUC; raised myopathy/rhabdomyolysis risk - use a non-CYP3A4 statin when possible)
Cyclosporine (cyclosporine dose often reduced 15-48% to maintain trough levels - monitor)
Rifampin or other CYP3A4 inducers (diltiazem levels can fall to undetectable - avoid)
moderate: Benzodiazepines midazolam and triazolam (AUC up 3-4 fold, prolonged sedation)
Buspirone (AUC up ~5.5-fold, Cmax up ~4.1-fold - may need dose reduction)
Cimetidine (raises diltiazem peak ~58% and AUC ~53% - may warrant dose adjustment)
Clonidine (sinus bradycardia, including cases needing pacemaker - monitor heart rate)
Quinidine (quinidine AUC increased ~51% - monitor and adjust)
Anesthetics (potentiated cardiac depression and vasodilation - titrate slowly)
minor: Ranitidine produced only small, nonsignificant increases in diltiazem levels
interactions.food: Oral extended-release capsules may be taken with or without food; swallow whole.
interactions.alcohol: Alcohol may add to hypotension and dizziness; advise caution.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause mild elevations of SGOT, SGPT, LDH, and alkaline phosphatase; hyperglycemia and hyperuricemia have been reported. Monitor hepatic and renal laboratory parameters at regular intervals.

serious: Congestive heart failure / worsening of preexisting LV dysfunction
Acute hepatic injury (significant transaminase/alkaline phosphatase elevations)
emergency: High-degree AV block with cardiac failure

monitoring: Blood pressure and heart rate (and ECG for AV block, especially with beta-blockers or digitalis)
Hepatic function (transaminases, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin), particularly during the first 1-8 weeks
Digoxin, cyclosporine, quinidine, or carbamazepine levels when co-administered
Signs and symptoms of worsening heart failure
counsel: Swallow the extended-release capsule whole; do not crush or chew
Do not stop the medicine suddenly without talking to your prescriber
Report dizziness, fainting, very slow heartbeat, or swelling of the ankles or feet
Sublingual nitroglycerin may still be used for acute chest pain during therapy
Report yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, or persistent skin rash
Tell your doctor and pharmacist about all other medicines, as diltiazem interacts with many drugs (statins, digoxin, cyclosporine, certain sedatives)
pk: IV bolus: rate-control response usually within 3 minutes; oral antihypertensive effect develops over chronic dosing
IV bolus: maximal heart rate reduction in 2-7 minutes; oral max antihypertensive effect usually by 14 days of chronic ER therapy
Extensively hepatically metabolized; blood levels vary over tenfold between patients
IV bolus heart-rate reduction lasts 1-3 hours; oral ER formulation supports once-daily dosing
Store at 25 C (77 F); excursions 15-30 C permitted; avoid excessive humidity
pearls: Non-dihydropyridine CCB: rate-limiting like verapamil, so it slows AV conduction - useful for atrial fibrillation/flutter rate control and PSVT termination (IV), unlike dihydropyridines
Distinguish formulations: oral ER capsules are for hypertension and angina; IV diltiazem is for acute supraventricular rate control - doses are not interchangeable
Avoid or use great caution combining with beta-blockers, especially in LV dysfunction or conduction disease, because of additive negative inotropic and chronotropic effects
Potent CYP3A4 inhibitor: raises levels of CYP3A4 statins (myopathy risk), cyclosporine, midazolam/triazolam, buspirone, carbamazepine, and quinidine
Contraindicated with systolic BP <90 mm Hg and in acute MI with pulmonary congestion
Acute hepatic injury, when it occurs, typically appears 1-8 weeks after starting and reverses on discontinuation
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose; in that case skip the missed dose and take the next one at the usual time. Do not take two doses at once to make up for a missed dose.
overdose: Reported overdoses range from <1 g to 18 g; events include bradycardia, hypotension, heart block, and cardiac failure, with most fatal cases involving multiple drugs. Because of extensive metabolism, blood levels vary widely and are of limited use, and diltiazem is not appreciably removed by peritoneal or hemodialysis (plasmapheresis or charcoal hemoperfusion may help). Provide supportive care and GI decontamination. Bradycardia: atropine 0.60-1.0 mg, then cautious isoproterenol if no response. High-degree AV block: treat as bradycardia; fixed block needs cardiac pacing. Cardiac failure: inotropes (isoproterenol, dopamine, dobutamine) and diuretics. Hypotension: vasopressors such as dopamine or norepinephrine. IV calcium has also been used.
